notes.meaning: Jonah was deeply displeased and became furious because God had mercy on Nineveh instead of destroying it. The people of Nineveh were bitter enemies of Israel, and Jonah wanted God to wipe them out. It was shocking that a prophet who had just received God's mercy in the belly of the fish would begrudge mercy to others.

Jonah prayed and admitted that this was the very reason he tried to flee to Tarshish in the first place. He was not afraid of failing; he was afraid that God would be kind and spare the city. He knew God was gracious, patient, full of loyal love, and eager to turn away judgment when sinners repent.

differ.view: Reformed Christians teach that God's eternal purposes never change, so God 'relenting' describes a change in his outward dealings with people rather than a change in his mind.
Many evangelicals teach that God's warnings of judgment are conditional, meaning God stays completely consistent when he spares people who turn from sin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars point out a Hebrew wordplay where the same verb is used for Nineveh turning from evil and God turning from sending disaster.

notes.meaning: Jonah begged God to take his life, claiming it was better for him to die than to keep living. He knew that life belongs to God alone and did not try to kill himself, yet his heart was full of bitter resentment. Disappointed pride can make even a servant of God wish for death rather than rejoice in God's will.

The Lord answered Jonah with a gentle question, asking if he had any right to be angry. God had the right to strike his rebellious prophet down, but he showed patient mercy instead. This question forced Jonah to see that his anger against God's compassion had no excuse.

Jonah went out to the east side of Nineveh, built a small shelter of branches, and sat in its shade. He stayed there waiting to see whether God might still send destruction upon the city. His hard heart made him hope for judgment even after the people had repented.

The Lord provided a broad-leafed plant that grew up quickly over Jonah to give him cooling shade and ease his discomfort. Jonah was filled with great joy over the plant, which was the first time in the story he felt happy. Even while dealing with a resentful prophet, God kindly tended to his physical needs.

At dawn the next day, God sent a worm that attacked the plant at its root, causing it to wither away. The same sovereign God who raised the plant had complete authority to take it away using a tiny insect. Earthly comforts can vanish in an instant when God wills it.

As the sun came up, God sent a scorching east wind while the sun beat fiercely on Jonah's head. The prophet felt faint from the terrible heat and again asked to die, saying death was better than life. God used these harsh conditions to expose how easily Jonah fell into despair over his own comfort.

God asked Jonah again whether he had any right to be angry, this time concerning the withered plant. Jonah angrily insisted that he had every right to be furious, even enough to die. He was blinded by self-pity and cared more about a plant than about an entire city of people.

The Lord pointed out that Jonah cared deeply about a plant he never worked for or helped grow. It had suddenly appeared in a single night and died just as quickly. Jonah was weeping over a worthless, short-lived shrub simply because it had shaded him.

God showed how much greater his own compassion was for the vast city of Nineveh. The city contained more than 120,000 little children too young to know their right hand from their left, along with many animals. God wants his people to share his heart of mercy toward a lost and hurting world.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern teachers explain the phrase about not knowing the right hand from the left as describing spiritually blind adults who could not make moral judgments, rather than young children.
